content: This document updates the previously published CDC recommendations for infection control practices in dentistry to incorporate new data, materials, technologies, and equipment. These updated recommendations aim to reduce the risk of disease transmission in dental settings, including transmission from patients to dental healthcare workers (DHCWs), from DHCWs to patients, and between patients. The principles of infection control remain unchanged, but advancements in technology, materials, and equipment necessitate ongoing evaluation of current practices. The unique nature of dental procedures, instrumentation, and patient care settings may require specific strategies to prevent the transmission of pathogens among DHCWs and their patients. These recommended practices apply to all settings where dental treatment is provided and should be observed alongside OSHA-mandated worker protection practices, such as those outlined in the final rule on occupational exposure to bloodborne pathogens. Dental patients and DHCWs may be exposed to various microorganisms through blood, oral, or respiratory secretions. These microorganisms include cytomegalovirus, hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), Mycobacterium tuberculosis, staphylococci, streptococci, and other bacteria and viruses, particularly those affecting the upper respiratory tract. Infections can be transmitted in dental settings through direct contact with blood, oral fluids, or other secretions; indirect contact with contaminated instruments, equipment, or surfaces; or contact with airborne contaminants in droplet spatter or aerosols. For an infection to occur, three conditions must be met: a susceptible host, a pathogen with sufficient infectivity and quantity to cause infection, and a portal of entry for the pathogen into the host. Effective infection control strategies aim to break one or more links in this chain of infection, thereby preventing disease transmission. Universal precautions, which extend blood and body fluid precautions to all patients, must be consistently applied in dental care. Specific actions are also recommended to reduce the risk of tuberculosis transmission in dental and other healthcare facilities. Although the risk of bloodborne infection transmission from DHCWs to patients is considered low, precise risks have not been quantified in dental settings through rigorous epidemiologic studies. Reports from 1970 to 1987 identified nine clusters of HBV transmission associated with infected DHCWs. Additionally, six cases of HIV transmission from a dentist to patients have been reported. Since 1987, no cases of HBV transmission from dentists to patients have been reported, likely due to improved adherence to universal precautions, routine glove use, and increased immunity from hepatitis B vaccination. HBV infection is uncommon among adults in the United States, but serologic surveys indicate that 10%-30% of healthcare and dental workers show evidence of past or present HBV infection. OSHA requires employers to provide hepatitis B vaccinations at no cost to employees who may be exposed to blood or infectious materials. The CDC also recommends that all workers, including DHCWs, who may be occupationally exposed to blood or blood-contaminated substances, be vaccinated against HBV. DHCWs are also at risk for exposure to other vaccine-preventable diseases, such as influenza, measles, mumps, rubella, and tetanus, and vaccination against these diseases may be appropriate. Protective attire and barrier techniques are essential in dental-care settings. Medical gloves (latex or vinyl) must always be worn when there is potential contact with blood, saliva, or mucous membranes. Nonsterile gloves are suitable for examinations and nonsurgical procedures, while sterile gloves should be used for surgical procedures. Gloves should be changed between patients, and hands should be washed before donning and after removing gloves. Gloves should not be washed, disinfected, or sterilized for reuse, as this can cause deterioration and compromise their integrity. Face shields or surgical masks and protective eyewear should be worn when splashing or spattering of blood or body fluids is likely. Masks should be changed between patients or when they become wet. Protective clothing, such as gowns or lab coats, should be worn when clothing is likely to be soiled with blood or body fluids and should be changed daily or when visibly soiled. Instruments used in dental procedures are classified as critical, semicritical, or noncritical based on their risk of transmitting infection. Critical instruments, such as forceps and scalpels, must be sterilized after each use. Semicritical instruments, such as mirrors, should also be sterilized, or at a minimum, receive high-level disinfection if sterilization is not feasible. Noncritical instruments, such as x-ray head components, may be disinfected with intermediateor low-level disinfectants. Sterilization or high-level disinfection of instruments requires thorough cleaning to remove debris. Instruments should be placed in water or disinfectant/detergent immediately after use to prevent drying of patient material. Heat-stable instruments should be sterilized using steam under pressure (autoclaving), dry heat, or chemical vapor. Instruments not used immediately should be packaged before sterilization. Manufacturer instructions for cleaning and sterilization should be followed closely. Dental unit surfaces and countertops should be cleaned and disinfected after each patient and at the end of the workday. Intermediate-level disinfectants, such as phenolics, iodophors, or chlorine-containing compounds, are recommended for surfaces contaminated with patient material. Fresh sodium hypochlorite solutions (household bleach diluted 1:100 with water) are effective and inexpensive but should be used cautiously due to their corrosive nature. Reusable dental instruments attached to air or water lines, such as ultrasonic scaler tips and air/water syringe tips, should be cleaned and sterilized after each patient. Disposable items, such as prophylaxis cups and saliva ejector tips, should be used for one patient only and discarded appropriately. Biopsy specimens should be placed in sturdy containers with secure lids to prevent leakage during transport. Care should be taken to avoid contaminating the outside of the container. If contamination occurs, the container should be cleaned and disinfected or placed in an impervious bag. Extracted teeth used in dental education should be considered infectious and handled with universal precautions. They should be cleaned of patient material, disinfected, and stored in a germicidal solution. Gloves and other protective equipment should be worn when handling extracted teeth, and work surfaces should be cleaned and disinfected after use. Waste materials contaminated with blood or body fluids should be disposed of according to established regulations. Liquid waste may be poured into drains connected to sanitary sewer systems, while solid waste should be placed in sealed, impervious bags to prevent leakage. Sharps should be placed intact into puncture-resistant containers before disposal.
